vignette:
At thirty-five, Minh is an accountant who came to the United States a decade ago, after surviving months of political torture in his home country. The details of what happened are still jumbled in his mind-he cannot put events in the right order, and so he has given up trying to tell the story. What remains is a film that plays over and over, always the same loop, always ending with him alone in a concrete room. The memory doesn't feel like his own; it belongs to someone else, a weaker version of himself he now barely recognizes.

Minh works in a mid-sized firm, seated in a quiet cubicle where he reviews spreadsheets and prepares tax projections for clients. He has learned to dread two things: new faces and talk of the future. When a stranger appears-a new hire, a client he has never met-his chest tightens. A single question about next quarter's goals or next year's retirement plan is enough to send an intrusive memory surging: the interrogator's calm voice asking about the future of a protest, and then the pain. For Minh, talking about tomorrow or encountering an unfamiliar person does not simply remind him of the past; it confirms a terrifying appraisal: *You can never know who will harm you.* Every stranger could be a threat, every future conversation a trap. He has come to believe that he has permanently changed for the worse-that the torture scarred something irreparable in him. And underneath that, a haunting thought recurs: *Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening.* Someone stronger, someone braver would have resisted or escaped, but he did not.

These appraisals do not sit separately from his memories; they reshape them. Because he believes he is permanently damaged, the memory of the event feels alien-it cannot belong to the person he is now, a man who flinches at a handshake. The conviction that others would have coped better makes the memory fragment: he cannot hold the sequence steady, cannot decide if his own actions were cowardly or simply human. The film replays, but each time the order shifts, leaving him more confused. He will be sitting at his desk, and a sudden image arrives-a guard's boot, the taste of blood-and he cannot tell if it happened before or after the electric wire. The replay is unstoppable, but its details slip through his fingers, as though the story belongs to a stranger.

Over the months, Minh's life has narrowed. He avoids discussing his own future with anyone, giving vague answers when a colleague asks about his weekend plans. He limits client meetings whenever possible, delegating face-to-face contact to a coworker. His divorce, two years ago, was partly a result of his inability to talk about where the relationship was heading or to meet his wife's friends-strangers all. He lives alone now, and the quiet of his apartment is both a relief and a cage.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a session with a new client who reminded him of an interrogator: same build, same way of tilting his head. Minh felt the memory crash in, and for two days he could not go to work. He is not sure he can be fixed. What frightens him most is the thought that he will never feel real again-that the permanent damage is, in fact, permanent. Yet part of him still hopes that if he can make the story straight, if he can find a way to look at the memory without flinching, maybe the film will stop. He is here to try.
